links.note: BCE stands for Before Common Era - this concept is where BC is replaced by Before Common Era or BCE for years counted backward.
A period of ten years is a decade - the decade is named in this concept's DON'T MISS OUT box alongside the century and the millennium.
A century holds 100 years - the unit this concept defines and then counts from the year 1 CE.
A millennium holds 1,000 years - the second of the two longer units in this concept's box.
Naming a literary source from Indian literature, such as the Vedas, is a question about the categories in the figure of the main sources of history that closes this concept.
Folklore and genealogical records are oral sources - a source-category judgement, which this concept's summary figure of the main sources of history supplies.
Early humans obtained food mainly by hunting and gathering - this concept states they were mainly hunters and gatherers, relying on hunting and collecting edible plants and fruits.
Early humans lived in temporary camps, rock shelters or caves - this concept's opening sentence, word for word, rather than the band-and-timescale concept.
Pottery as the new technology for making pots and other clay objects appears in this concept's list of new technologies.
Copper as the first metal used for durable tools - this concept states copper first and iron later.
A hamlet is a small settlement or small village - the gloss this concept carries where hamlets grow into sizeable villages.
Afterlife glossed as a life that begins after death sits in this concept, beside the statement that early ancestors had beliefs about natural elements and possibly some notion of afterlife.
How understanding the past helps us understand the present world is verbatim the THINK ABOUT IT question in this concept, following the Carr quotation about the present and the past.
The difference between a geologist studying the Earth's physical features and a palaeontologist studying fossils - both definitions come from this concept's four experts.
Why Common Era replaced AD for dating - this concept explains that AD, the Latin phrase for years after Jesus' birth, is now called the Common Era or CE across the world.
Counting the years between 100 BCE and 100 CE as 199 because there is no year zero - this concept is the one that teaches add them but subtract 1.
How a time line helps in understanding historical events - this concept's point that a timeline shows a sequence of dates and events and the order in which they took place.
Defining oral sources and giving two examples is a question about the source categories this concept's closing figure brings together, not about the historian who weighs them.
Scientific studies contributing to reconstruction of the past - studies of ancient climates, chemical studies of excavated materials and genetics of ancient people are listed only in this concept.

What can be inferred from rock paintings made by early humans - this concept holds the rock paintings found in hundreds of caves, some simple figures or symbols, others scenes with animals or humans. Already linked and correct.
How the end of the last Ice Age impacted settlement patterns - warming climate, improved living conditions, people settling down and cultivating. Already linked and correct.
Why early agricultural communities settled near rivers - this concept gives both water and more fertile soil as the reasons, in those terms.
A historian is a person who studies and writes about the past - this concept's opening sentence, which no other concept in the chapter carries.
Fossils as impressions of footprints or parts of plants or animals preserved within layers of soil or rocks - glossed in this concept beside the palaeontologist.
The Gregorian calendar's leap year every four years and the century-year rule that only multiples of 400 qualify - the arithmetic exception this concept sets out. Already linked and correct.

The significance of monuments as archaeological sources rests on this concept's claim that every object or structure tells a story and is like a piece in a jigsaw puzzle, and on its figure of the main sources of history.
Afterlife in the context of early human beliefs - this concept's carefully hedged sentence about beliefs concerning natural elements and possibly some notion of afterlife.
Domestication of animals - this concept says they also domesticated animals such as cattle and goats once they started settling down and cultivating.
How pottery benefited settled communities with containers for storing food - pottery for making pots and other clay objects is one of the new technologies this concept introduces.
Welfare in the context of early community leaders - this concept has chieftains responsible for the well-being of the people, with welfare glossed as health, prosperity and well-being.
E.H. Carr's unending dialogue between the present and the past, and why studying history matters - this concept opens on that quotation. Already linked and correct.
Explaining the BCE/CE system and the add-then-subtract-1 span calculation because there is no year zero - this concept's whole second half.
The jigsaw puzzle analogy and the missing pieces is this concept's own metaphor, including the statement that in history quite a few pieces of the puzzle may remain missing.
Describing the archaeological, literary, oral and artistic categories of historical sources with an example of each is exactly the figure of the main sources of history that closes this concept.
The role of the end of the last Ice Age in the development of agriculture and settlement - the climate explanation this concept is built on. Already linked and correct.
The importance of fire and tool-making for early humans - this concept has them using fire and making improved stone axes and blades and arrowheads, the two advances the question pairs.
The gradual growth of social complexity from bands through hamlets and villages to small towns, with chieftains, exchange, pottery and metal - this concept narrates that whole sequence.

Imagining yourself as an archaeologist excavating a settlement and listing the artefacts to look for - this concept's own list of tools, pots, beads, figurines, bones and parts of houses is what the answer draws on.

How ancient art such as rock paintings contributes when written records are scarce - this concept holds both the rock paintings and the fact that these groups' languages are now lost because nothing was written. Already linked and correct.

Why historians must be critical of sources and acknowledge bias and limitation - this concept is the one where sources sometimes confirm each other and sometimes contradict, and the historian has to decide which source to trust more.
The panchanga as a book of astronomical tables predicting eclipses, sunrise and sunset and festival timings - this concept's closing box on Indian calendars. Already linked and correct.

The recent appearance of Homo sapiens against the whole span of Earth's history - this concept's sentence that 300,000 years appears very long yet is only a tiny fraction of the Earth's history is the implication the question asks for. Already linked and correct.

Harappan 2500 BCE against Ashoka 268 BCE, and how many years ago Ashoka reigned counting from 2025 CE - the load-bearing step is this concept's rule that a BCE and a CE date are added and 1 subtracted because there is no year zero. The timeline concept would only cover which event is older.

A historian comparing a merchant's letters and account books with European travelogues, and deciding what to do when they conflict - this concept's method of consulting as many sources as possible and judging which to trust when they contradict. The source-category concept classifies but does not resolve a conflict.

A burial with clay pots, bronze spearheads and semi-precious beads against a grave with only simple pots - the bronze spearheads and the unequal grave goods both test this concept's pottery, metal and growing social complexity, which is where the chapter's account of individual versus collective standing sits.
